baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Introduced organisms and pathogens as causes in colonial history: the Columbian exchange (1972) and ecological imperialism (1986)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Crosby's own statement, Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue (pp. 1–7 read; 2004-edition pagination). It opens: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation' (p. 2), and names 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes' (p. 2). Underlying the pull of these lands 'were factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5). 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'Perhaps European humans have triumphed because of their superiority in arms, organization, and fanaticism, but what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). The contents give chapters 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171) and 'Ills' (195). His 1978 American Heritage essay on Plymouth (web text read in full; no print pages) makes the disease argument for New England: 'Disease was among the commodities, and in this trade the Indians would come off second best'; 'Innocent of immunity or experience, the Indians were helpless'; the Pilgrims survived 'thanks more to biology than religion'. In-period reception inside the field: Cronon's 1993 ASEH address (read) turns the two books into lessons of environmental history, 'When people migrate from one ecosystem to another, they carry with them other organisms—plants, animals, microbes—whose success or failure in the new location is often crucial in determining the success or failure of the migration' (p. 8) and 'Beware of bugs that come from afar' (p. 10), both footnoted to The Columbian Exchange and Ecological Imperialism (nn. 16, 25, p. 22). Cook's 1990 essay, read, takes The Columbian Exchange as the model for an ecological reading of Canadian contact: 'As Alfred W. Crosbie [sic], Jr., demonstrated so brilliantly nearly two decades ago ... contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13, n. 35). Miller's 1987 review (Medical History, read in full) calls the book 'a vividly written account of ecological transition' and finds Crosby 'careful not to overestimate the significance of any single component' (p. 374). The ASEH's history page (undated institutional account, read) records him commenting on the keynote at the society's first conference (Irvine, 1982) and lists him among 'founding members of our society such as Don Worster, Susan Flader, Alfred Crosby, and Opie himself'. A contribution, not a founding: no text read calls him the founder. Melville's adaptation of his question to Mexico (1994) is recorded in the existing melville_plague note, not rechecked. McNeill (2003, pp. 24, 33) and Isenberg (2013, p. 86), with their criticism of determinism, are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Ecological change at world scale: the biological expansion of Europe and the making of Neo-Europes, 900–1900 (1986)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The scale and question of Ecological Imperialism (1986), prologue and contents (read; 2004-edition pagination). Other peoples expanded into adjacent lands, but 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe' to Neo-Europes, 'lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); the book runs from 'The Norse and the Crusaders' and 'The Fortunate Isles' through 'Winds' to 'New Zealand' (contents, pp. xi–xii), and asks whether 'the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). He thanks 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (acknowledgments, p. xxii); McNeill is the world-history synthesiser on the global entry. In-period uptake by connected history: Subrahmanyam (1997, p. 738, re-read) lists among early modern shifts 'travel, discovery and colonization as leading to an ecological shift of global dimensions', and his note 10 points to 'the oft-cited (and oft-criticized) works of Alfred Crosby (The Columbian Exchange, and Ecological Imperialism)', adding that Grove's Green Imperialism 'pays far greater attention to Asia than does Crosby'. A contribution, not a founding, and a resource with stated limits: Subrahmanyam's own note marks it as criticised and as giving Asia less attention than Grove. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: McNeill (2003, p. 32) calls it 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories'; Crosby's 2004 preface names Pomeranz's Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (pp. xvii, xx).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Crosby and Melville connect introduced organisms with colonial expansion; Grove traces conservation through colonial networks; after 2000 McNeill's Something New Under the Sun (2000) and, with Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016) write the twentieth century and the Anthropocene at world scale
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Ecological change and cross-border material relations provide one route beyond national containers; examples require attention to scale. Crosby’s temperate regions, Melville’s Mexican case and Grove’s island networks operate at different scales. Their books provide resources for histories across borders; this does not prove that all global historians adopted them. Subrahmanyam738n10 explicitly cites Crosby and Grove, adding named primary reception for this route; it does not establish every proposed Melville reception. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_112 revision): the Harvard University Press description of The Great Acceleration read ('The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene'; 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated the Anthropocene'); McNeill 2000 by metadata and prizes only.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Ecological change as a two-way relation of people and nature, traced through property, markets and ideas of nature (1983–1995); and the field's institutions: ASEH president 1989–93, editor of the Weyerhaeuser Environmental Books 1994–2014 ('acquiring, editing, and writing forewords for all titles'), and in 2013 'the first self-described environmental historian ever to serve as president of the AHA'
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cronon’s own in-period statements. Changes in the Land (1983), ch. 1 'The View from Walden', read in full in an unpaginated web transcription (page numbers not verified): 'The replacement of Indians by predominantly European populations in New England was as much an ecological as a cultural revolution'; 'An ecological history begins by assuming a dynamic and changing relationship between environment and culture, one as apt to produce contradictions as continuities. Moreover, it assumes that the interactions of the two are dialectical'; 'The choice is not between two landscapes, one with and one without a human influence; it is between two human ways of living, two ways of belonging to an ecosystem'; 'The pig was not merely a pig but a creature bound among other things to the fence, the dandelion, and a very special definition of property'; a 'world capitalist system' draws people 'into trade and market relations which lie well beyond the boundaries of their local ecosystems'. He sets this against species-transfer accounts 'as Alfred Crosby and William H. McNeill have done', which are 'bound to be incomplete', and against functionalist ecological anthropology, which risks 'a static and ahistorical view'. In 1992 he calls Nature’s Metropolis 'a natural sequel' to that book, which 'described a comparable set of environmental changes that occurred in New England as that region became linked to London’s markets' (Annals of Iowa forum, p. 517). 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993): the lesson 'When people buy and sell things in a market, they link together ecosystems and encourage change' is 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14, citing Changes in the Land, Nature’s Metropolis and 'Kennecott Journey'); 'The chief moral of my own version of environmental history is the one I tried to embed in the title of my book Changes in the Land. To live as human beings on this planet is to change the world around us' (p. 19); 'the material history of environmental change is simultaneously a spiritual history of human consciousness and a political economic history of human society' (p. 19); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14), held together with the claim that 'the natural world exists quite apart from what we believe about it' (p. 15). 'Kennecott Journey' (1992, p. 33): 'The special task of environmental historians is to tell stories that carry us back and forth across the boundary between people and nature to reveal just how culturally constructed that boundary is—and how dependent upon natural systems it remains.' 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995, author’s reflow p. 1): wilderness is 'quite profoundly a human creation'. A contribution, not a founding: he makes the claim for materialist analysis that tries 'to finesse a full-blown determinism' on behalf of the field ('One important contribution of environmental history', 1993, p. 13), and places the field among the 'new' histories of the 1960s (p. 2). Contested in period: Danbom (1992) reads Nature’s Metropolis for its 'environmental moralism' (p. 503) and as 'a book about evil unleavened by good' (p. 506); Cronon answers 'I see no pure heroes or pure villains in the stories I tell' (p. 522). His 1990 JAH response to Worster is unread. The 2003 afterword (pp. 182–185: property analysis learned from anthropology, economics and legal theory; his own criticism of schematic capitalism and source asymmetry) is a later reading. edge_342 (anthropology → environment) and edge_343 (environment → culture) stay: they record anthropology as a resource and environmental history’s contribution to cultural history; this arrow is his own framework. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_901 revision): CV pp. 2, 14–15 read in full; the AHA's open text of 'Storytelling' read in passages.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990); and, at the end, the 'Second Earth' of 1500 whose abundance gave 'the false impression that there was no limit' (Shrinking the Earth, 2016, as read by Collomb)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_904 revision): Collomb 2017 para. 2 read in full; Shrinking the Earth itself unread; the Origins page (Hall chair from 1989 until retirement) and the AHA award list (2012) read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009), developed into a distinction between globe and planet (2015–22)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here through their abstract, which holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis", and through his reports; the body of their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history. Later work, added in revision 1.151: the Tanner Lectures (2015, read in part) distinguish humanity as "homo" from the scientists' "anthropos" and conclude that "we have fallen into 'deep' history"; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021; publisher's page and contents; unread) is summarised in his own words: "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 593). In environmental history's own journal, Atte Arffman (Environment and History, 2022, read) writes that "historians can no longer dismiss material realities and non-human world" and that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The criticisms of the species category and of the divide's novelty are now drawn separately (environment → Chakrabarty; science → Chakrabarty).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: An ecological interpretation of early Canadian history: contact as the interaction of ecologies, 'cabbages, at least as much as kings' (1990)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Reuses the reading recorded on 2026-10-13 for the environment-family drafts (pe131_extras_cook_1990; canon-evidence-canada.md, text C1). It was not re-read for this entry because Project MUSE refused automated access. Cook's W. L. Morton Lecture (Trent, October 1990; JCS 25:4, 1990–91) starts from Morton's 1946 remark that history 'is concerned with ecology too' (p. 5): 'It is an insight which I would like to try to build upon' (p. 6). He marks a break with the staple historians: 'for this earlier generation of historians the exploitation of the environment was accepted as natural and necessary, even though excesses might be deplored' (pp. 6–7), while 'More recent environmental historians have a different focus. They are no longer much concerned with explaining the impact of the environment on man; it is the impact of man on nature that is at the centre of their work' (p. 7). Following Crosby, 'contact was even more significantly the interaction of different ecologies or environments' (p. 13). His conclusion: 'Cabbages, at least as much as kings, led to the transformation of the new world' (p. 15, as recorded in canon-evidence-canada.md; not in the source's verification note). In-period reading: Gauvreau (Acadiensis 1991, pp. 164–165 n. 12), arguing about Cook's religious history, called the lecture his 'recent “conversion experience” concerning the happy convergence of nature and culture'. Later reading, labelled: Wynn (2004, p. 33, recorded in pe131_extras_wynn_2004) quotes Cook's claim that Canadian historical writing 'has always been concerned with the environment' to describe Canadians who 'seemed to wonder what all the fuss was about'. A contribution, not a founding. edge_913 (harold_a_innis → environment) carries his continuity claim and Forkey's 1998 rejection of it; this edge carries his own ecological reading of contact.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: 'Modes of Prophecy and Production' answered Worster's 1990 agroecological programme (unread; reported by Isenberg 2013); 'A Place for Stories' (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy', set against Bonnifield's progressive plot
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: 'A Place for Stories' pp. 1347–1349 and 1363–1364 read (graph record pe131_cronon_place_stories_1992): the 'chief agent' and 'apocalyptic prophecy' sentences are at p. 1363, Worster's few pages on Indians at p. 1364. The 1990 response (JAH 76:4, 1122–31) is unread (OUP 403) and is known through Isenberg 2013, pp. 88–89 (read, graph record pe131_crosby_isenberg_2013); Cronon's CV p. 7 confirms the citation. A critique by reading, not a rejection: Cronon's essay treats both plots as narrative choices.

assessment: Two existing field edges already carry careful and substantial reception, but no individual neighbours. Three proposed edges make three mapped individual neighbours visible through specific primary uses or responses. One Crosby–Worster record retains two different intellectual actions with both witnesses: Worster uses Crosby’s concept; Crosby separately endorses Worster’s agroecological agenda. Both are Crosby-to-Worster contributions as phrased, so they are consolidated rather than duplicated. Neither is a generic school-membership claim. Later Pomeranz self-positioning is explicitly dated 2004. Strong absent-endpoint or inaccessible-body leads are held, not disproved. This is bounded whole-person research, not proof of an exhaustive network or a degree target.
preservation: No canonical edits, old qualification replacement, endpoint retargets, new biographies, chronology edits, raw-corpus changes or life/reading changes. Old group routes remain mixed and intact.
consolidation_note: Independent premerge review identified two proposed Crosby→Worster contribution records for the same directed pair. They were consolidated, retaining both claims, source IDs, locators and limits. No kind or direction was changed to avoid the guard.
